Review of “Stratospheric precursor induces wintertime phase reversal of the “Warm Arctic-Cold Eurasia” pattern” by Zhang et al. This study identifies a stratospheric precursor for the phase shift of the “Warm Arctic-Cold Eurasia” (WACE) pattern in winters. Composite analysis suggests that the sign change in stratospheric anomalies over North America precedes the WACE phase shift by about 25 days. Wave diagnostics suggest that the stratospheric variability facilitates the development of circulation and temperature anomalies over Eurasia. Climate models from CMIP6 generally support the observational results. However, this linkage appears to be missing in low-top models. I find the key points interesting, providing fresh perspectives on the role of the stratosphere in winter climate. But as I explain below, I have several major and minor concerns, mainly regarding the interpretation of the results and the clarity of the methods. In addition, it requires careful, thorough proofreading and language editing in both the main text and the supplementary information. General comments In my opinion, framing the stratospheric variation as an intensity change in the stratospheric polar vortex over North America is confusing and potentially misleading. The intensity of the stratospheric polar vortex is widely studied and is commonly described by the strength of its westerly winds, which reflect the polar vortex's overall intensity. The stratospheric anomalies analyzed here appear to be asymmetric, especially in early winter (Figure 1a). The current description of regional polar vortex intensity is confusing and does not connect well with the literature on the polar vortex, especially given that the significant anomalies appear outside of the vortex edge in the plot. In my opinion, in the years of CAWE to WACE, the morphology of the polar vortex undergoes an evident change. It appears to be stretched towards North America from early to late winter, in contrast to the contraction from a stretched shape during WACE to CAWE years. A stretched polar vortex, characterized by zonally asymmetric anomalies in the stratosphere, has been associated with cold anomalies over Eurasia in both observations and climate models (see Fig. 6 in Zou et al., 2023, Fig. 1 in Ding et al., 2023). On a related note, the discussion on the stratosphere’s downward influence requires major revisions. The authors ambiguously describe it as the stratospheric signal propagates downward into the troposphere, potentially confusing the mechanism of a weak polar vortex with a stretched polar vortex or strong stratospheric waves. Following a weak polar vortex, the downward propagation of negative zonal wind anomalies (negative NAM) may be amplified by tropospheric synoptic eddy feedbacks, thereby inducing midlatitude coldness. During polar vortex stretching, vertical wave coupling and planetary wave reflection are likely responsible for the changes in the tropospheric circulation. Reply to Reviewer #2: Review of Zhang et al.: “Stratospheric precursor induces wintertime phase reversal of the “Warm Arctic-Cold Eurasia” pattern” In the present study, Zhang et al. investigate the relationship between stratospheric polar vortex variability over North America and the phase reversals of the so-called Warm Arctic-Cold Eurasia (WACE) pattern during boreal winter. Rather than individual polar vortex or WACE events, the authors focus on winters where the stratospheric polar vortex over North America transitions from a negative geopotential height anomaly to a positive anomaly (or vice versa). This transition over time is then linked to a corresponding transition of the WACE pattern at the surface, with a lag of a few weeks. In a set of supplementary analyses, based on wave activity flux diagnostics, the authors argue that Rossby waves propagate downward from the stratosphere to the troposphere, thereby modulating the strength of the Ural blocking and the associated surface temperature anomalies over Eurasia. The relationship is further explored in climate models from CMIP6, where the authors find that models with a higher model top tend to better capture the observed relationship. The study addresses a quite specific topic, focusing on phase reversals of the WACE pattern, as opposed to individual events. The long timescales involved are interesting, as the coupled stratosphere-troposphere evolution is assessed over an entire winter, making it relevant for (sub) seasonal prediction. The quality of the figure presentation is generally very good. Furthermore, clear efforts have been made to provide a comprehensive analysis including various diagnostics, fields, and models. However, the overall clarity of the presentation needs substantial improvement. The manuscript is fairly dense, and I found it sometimes difficult to follow the analyses. In particular, the event definitions for the composites need to be described more clearly. Furthermore, the manuscript would benefit from careful language editing. In several places, the phrasing is unclear enough to make it difficult to follow the authors’ intended meaning. I have some more general comments, followed by a list of more specific comments. Reply: We have made clearer phrasing and careful revising for the language expression of the article. The previously unclear methods and definitions have all been added in the main text and the methods section. To address the issue of article density, we have used shorter sentences and more concise paragraphs to express our content, thereby enhancing readability. 1. This pattern can be identified in the second EOF mode of the winter SAT over the Arctic-northern Eurasia region, indicating that it is a dominant mode. The formation mechanism of the WACE pattern is complex, including the atmospheric response to changes in Arctic Sea ice and tropical-subtropical SST (Mori et al., 2019; Matsumura et al., 2019), as well as the internal atmospheric dynamics (Blackport et al., 2022; Ku et al., 2025) Fig. R2. In these 16 years, the stratospheric precursor could be found in 12 of them, which indicates that the physical mechanism of the WACE phase reversals is extremely complex and is not solely influenced by the stratosphere. Previous studies have revealed that the WACE phase reversal can be influenced by the reversal of the tropospheric Ural high in late December (Xu et al., 2022), which can be associated with the differences of the impact of autumn Arctic sea ice on the climate in early and late winter (Lü et al., 2019). Reply： As we pointed out in the response to the comment 2, there are many climate factors influencing the formation of WACE pattern and its phase reversal, not just the stratosphere. For this reason, we did not construct a comprehensive prediction model for the variation of WACE in the previous version. Based on your hint, we attempted to quantify the improvement in predicting the WACE pattern by incorporating the observed stratospheric signals into the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (EC) results. After adding the stratospheric prediction signal, the prediction results have indeed improved significantly, which also confirms the importance of this new stratospheric signal that we have discovered. The correlation coefficients between predicted and observed WACE index increase from 0.39 to 0.52 for early winter and from 0.31 to 0.50 for late winter during 1979–2023. To truly predict the subseasonal to seasonal variations of the WACE pattern, it is necessary to comprehensively consider multiple signals, including the stratosphere and tropical sea surface temperatures. The following are the specific details. (1) Our findings indicate that the phase transition of stratospheric anomalies over North America between Nov1Dec15 and Dec16Feb10 can induce a phase reversal of the WACE pattern between early winter (Dec1Jan10) and late winter (Jan11Feb28). The prediction information from the stratosphere based on our findings is that the daily evolution of stratospheric signals from November 1st to February 10th can provide the predictive information for the variation of WACE phase and intensity in winter (December 1st– February 28th). The reversal point of the stratospheric precursor leads that of WACE by approximately 25 days, corresponding to a predictive time scale of about 25 days. (2) Based on the daily SAT predictions from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (EC), we incorporate the stratospheric precursor signals into the EC forecast to examine whether our findings can improve the subseasonal-to-seasonal perdition skill of winter SAT over the Arctic and the mid-high latitude Eurasia. Specifically, a multiple linear regression correction is applied at each grid using the PV anomaly over North America (NAPV ) averaged in the preceding 20–25 days as predictors. The SAT in early winter IPV predicted by the EC forecast is released in November, while for late winter, the predicted SAT released in December are used. For example, by using the mean NAPV index from IPV November 1st–5th and the SAT forecast for December 1st from the EC model released in November, an improved SAT prediction for December 1st is obtained through a multiple linear regression. The improved SAT prediction for December 2nd to January 10th are adjusted analogously. For SAT prediction in late winter (January 11–February 28), the EC forecast data released in December are used, and the method of incorporating the stratospheric predictive signal remains the same. After incorporating the stratospheric signal, the predictive skill for SAT over the Arctic and the mid-high latitude Eurasia region shows improvement in both early and late winter (Fig. R3). The averaged correlation coefficient between predictions and observations in early winter on each grid increases from 0.56 to 0.60 for Arctic, and from 0.1 to 0.35 for Eurasia. For late winter, the correlation coefficients between predictions and observations increases from 0.52 to 0.57 for the Arctic and from 0.1 to 0.37 for Eurasia. The predictive performance for the WACE index during 1979–2023 also improved. The correlation coefficients between T predicted and observed WACET increased from 0.39 to 0.52 for early winter and from 0.31 to 0.50 for late winter. This improvement indicates that the changes in stratospheric anomalies provide effective prediction information, and confirms the importance of this new stratospheric signal that we proposed.
